# The N.F.L. Player Who Left Football for Math

John Urschel left the game in part because of health risks. Now he’s scoring points in a new profession, but A.I. looms as a different kind of career hazard.

![A person with a beard stands in an office between two windows. They wear a black sweater and dark jeans with one hand in their pocket.](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/12/01/multimedia/26SCI-CONVERSATION-URSCHEL1-jpht/26SCI-CONVERSATION-URSCHEL1-jpht-articleLarge.jpg?quality=75&auto=avif&disable=upscale)

John Urschel at his home in Belmont, Mass., this month. Credit... Lucy Lu for The New York Times

By Siobhan Roberts

Nov. 26, 2026

John Urschel, a former N.F.L. offensive lineman, doesn’t have much time for football these days. Now a professor of mathematics at M.I.T., he generally follows college games but not the pros: “Watching football Saturday and Sunday is asking far too much of my wife,” he said in an interview this week. Mostly he pays attention to Virginia Tech (his best friend is their offensive coordinator) and Penn State (his alma mater). On Thanksgiving Day he expects to be “kid wrangling,” not parked in front of the television.

After playing three seasons for the Baltimore Ravens, from 2014 to 2016, Dr. Urschel retired at age 26 to finish a Ph.D. in mathematics. He published a memoir in 2019, “ Mind and Matter: A Life in Math and Football,” which he wrote with his wife, the writer Louisa Thomas. It appeared on the New York Times best-seller list for sports and fitness books.

In recent months, as new research has seemed to confirm football’s long-term occupational health risks, the profession of mathematics is experiencing a different sort of crisis. Artificial intelligence systems have generated solutions — collaborating, to various degrees, with human mathematicians — to some of math’s most illustrious and elusive problems.

Dr. Urschel is one of those mathematicians. In August, he and Rikhav Shah, a postdoctoral researcher at M.I.T., posted a significant result to arXiv, an online prepublication platform. As the authors described in their “A.I. usage statement” at the end of the paper, this research “blends purely human-based mathematics with some mathematics that involved the use of ChatGPT Sol 5.6 and Claude Fable 5.” Then, early last month, Dr. Urschel posted an even more significant paper — this time around, he used OpenAI’s ChatGPT Sol 5.6 and Astra 6 when he was stumped. The research resolved a well-known conjecture posed in the mid-1990s by the mathematician Nick Trefethen.

One of Dr. Urschel’s mentors, Peter Sarnak of the Institute for Advanced Study and Princeton University, called the October paper “a great result.” He suggested that Dr. Urschel’s targeted use of A.I. — to get across the finish line on specific points rather than to put out an amorphous, unintelligible proof — might serve as a new paradigm for math research.

Dr. Urschel isn’t sure: “What does this mean for early-career researchers? What does this mean for postdocs, for grad students, for undergrads?” he asked.
